climate-energy-51e1f920c0.headline: Is India’s solar power play facing its Icarus moment?
climate-energy-51e1f920c0.fulltext:
New Delhi: For a country that recorded all of the world’s 50 hottest cities this April, India’s ability to harness the sun’s energy took decades to take off. It wasn’t until 2011-12 that the country crossed a critical milestone: 1 gigawatt of installed solar power capacity. The next significant milestone was 100 GW, achieved more than a decade later, in early 2025.
India has galloped since, adding nearly 50GW of solar power capacity in 2025 and reaching 168.04GW by 31 August this year. It’s a stellar achievement. But it is beginning to strain the country’s vast electricity grid.
India’s transmission infrastructure is struggling to carry all the electricity generated when the sun shines. Surplus solar power can congest the grid, while inadequate storage means excess energy cannot always be saved for use when demand rises.
At the same time, fluctuations in solar power generation, depending on the time of day and weather, make it harder to balance electricity supply and demand, and maintain the grid’s frequency within the permitted range. If operators cannot correct such imbalances, the risk of wider disruptions increases.
In some instances, grid operators have asked solar farms to reduce or stop generation, a process known as curtailment, even when sunshine is abundant.
No easy solution is in sight, threatening to hamper one of the world’s largest energy transition efforts—from fossil fuels to clean energy—by the world’s third-largest generator of renewable energy.
“We are seeing increasing stress on the grid, particularly in the form of transmission congestion, renewable energy curtailment, and greater balancing requirements,” said Prashant Sinha, chief executive of Resonia Ltd, a power transmission firm. “However, these operational stresses should not automatically be characterized as grid instability.”
Changing priorities
As India’s green energy drive enters its next phase, the focus has turned to strengthening the country’s electricity infrastructure. This includes building adequate capacity to carry electricity from solar and wind farms to the power grid and then to factories, homes and other consumers.
Consequently, installing new renewable energy capacity has taken a back seat. About 14.7GW of renewable energy projects were awarded in FY26, down from 40.6GW in FY25 and 47.3GW in FY24, according to rating agency Icra. The slowdown has continued this fiscal year, with only 4.7GW awarded as of 10 August.
On the other hand, 4,301 circuit kilometres (ckm) of transmission capacity was installed in the first five months of this fiscal year (April–August), according to data from the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), the country’s apex power-sector planning body. That is 58% of the 7,403 ckm target for FY27.
In February last year, the CEA advised state power utilities and renewable energy implementation agencies to incorporate two-hour co-located energy storage systems, equivalent to 10% of installed solar project capacity, in future solar tenders.
On 3 September this year, the authority proposed mandating two-hour battery energy storage systems (BESS), with capacity equivalent to at least 10% of installed capacity, for all new solar and onshore wind projects commissioned after 1 July 2027. These systems can store solar and wind energy when it is generated for use later.
India currently has only 8.6 gigawatt hour (GWh) of BESS capacity. Another 42.53 GWh is under construction, 38.42 GWh has been awarded, and 65.57 GWh is in the tendering process. That amounts to 155.12 GWh of existing and planned BESS capacity, while the CEA projects a requirement of 236 GWh by 2032.
India also has a it at various stages of development. These plants can absorb surplus renewable power during off-peak hours and release it when demand rises. The CEA has a roadmap to install another 100GW of pumped storage project (PSP) capacity by 2035-36.
Sustaining momentum
In the first six months of FY27 (April–September), India added 24.56GW of renewable energy capacity, including 20.79GW of solar and 3.11GW of wind capacity, show data from the Union ministry of new and renewable energy (MNRE).
Overall, India had 308.02GW of installed non-fossil fuel-based electricity capacity as of 30 September, including 299.24GW of renewable energy capacity. Another 183.14GW is under implementation, while 51.29GW has been tendered. India is targeting 500GW of non-fossil fuel-based power capacity by 2030.
“The idea is to sustain the current momentum. We have achieved about 50GW of RE in a year. The idea should be to continue this momentum and keep on increasing from here,” MNRE secretary Santosh Kumar Sarangi said in a recent interview with Mint.
“If you go by CEA’s projection then by 2035-36, another 400GW of RE is expected to be added. And the confidence for this comes because the battery energy storage system cost has also gone down. So if more and more RE has to come then more of BESS, more of PSP will have to supplement RE,” he added.
An MNRE spokesperson said the ministry’s focus was on expanding transmission infrastructure, improving forecasting and scheduling, and coordinating with the ministry of power, the CEA, state governments and utilities to minimize congestion and renewable energy curtailment.
“India’s energy transition is moving from capacity addition towards delivering reliable, affordable and round-the-clock green power,” the spokesperson said in an email reply to Mint’s queries.
“We are promoting round-the-clock (RTC), firm and dispatchable renewable energy (FDRE), and solar-wind hybrid projects integrated with storage to ensure that renewable electricity is available in line with demand, including during evening and peak hours,” the spokesperson added. “Battery energy storage systems and pumped storage hydropower will play a critical role in balancing the variability of renewable energy.”
While solar power will continue to be complemented by wind, small hydro and other renewable energy sources, the spokesperson said “timely signing of power purchase agreements and power sale agreements, along with effective project implementation, will also be essential to translate awarded capacity into operational projects”.
The spokesperson also noted that the CEA’s March 2026 transmission plan envisages transmission infrastructure to integrate more than 900GW of non-fossil capacity by 2035-36.
“India’s energy transition is entering a more demanding phase. The focus is no longer limited to adding renewable capacity; it is equally about ensuring the grid can integrate and deliver that clean power when and where it is needed,” said Simarpreet Singh, CEO of Hartek Power, an engineering, procurement, and construction company focused on the power and solar sectors.
Solar surge
India moved from treating solar power as a rural-electrification technology and a corporate social responsibility initiative to making it a central pillar of its energy system. However, for several years solar power remained expensive with no real progress in terms of installation.
The Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission launched in January 2010 provided some support, starting with modest targets of 1GW of grid-connected solar in Phase I and enhancing it to a 100GW solar target for 2022.
The Solar Parks Scheme, introduced in 2014, brought about much of the push for solar power as it aimed to resolve a key bottleneck: land. Instead of every developer separately acquiring land, obtaining clearances and building transmission connections, solar parks could provide common roads, substations and transmission infrastructure.
The scale-up thereafter was extraordinary—from about 2.8GW of installed solar capacity at the end of March 2014 to 168.04GW as on 31 August 2026. Of this, about 124GW were ground-mounted projects, 32.6GW were grid-connected rooftop solar units, 4.8GW were solar components in hybrid projects, and 6.6GW off-grid solar.
The launch of the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana in February 2024, the flagship scheme to install 30GW of rooftop solar capacity at a cost of about ₹1 crore, also contributed to a pickup in solar installation. However, it has not added to grid strain because it primarily caters to households, and only excess power can be sold to the discoms.
By 2018, India’s investment of $20 billion in adding solar power capacity was greater than the investment in all fossil-fuel electricity generation combined, according to the International Energy Agency. In 2022, around $15 billion was invested in Indian solar capacity, marking a revival from Covid-hit FY21.
More broadly, India’s clean-energy investment reached $68 billion in 2023, almost 40% above its 2016–20 average, while in 2024 an extraordinary 83% of power-sector investment, about $100 billion, went to clean energy.
Cost of constraints
According to Ember, a Norway-based think tank focused on energy transition, transmission constraints led to the loss of 300 GWh of clean electricity in India in the first quarter of 2026 (January–March), particularly at grid pooling stations in the northern and western regions.
On 30 March alone, India lost 34 GWh of clean generation, equivalent to the daily electricity use of about 5 million urban middle-class households, Ember said in a report in May.
The analysis also found that total renewable energy curtailment in Q1 2026 reached around 470 GWh, of which 300 GWh stemmed directly from transmission constraints. The northern region accounted for 178 GWh and the western region for 122 GWh. The southern region recorded none, reflecting better synchronisation between generation and grid expansion.
Duttatreya Das, Ember’s energy analyst for Asia, said India’s renewable energy curtailment arising from transmission constraints is beginning to reach “materially significant levels”.
Inadequate transmission capacity has left about 40GW of power purchase agreements (PPAs) and power sale agreements (PSAs) unsigned, according to the Ember report. This 40GW of capacity, mostly solar, lacks integrated storage and is therefore less attractive to electricity distribution companies, or discoms, as the power is unavailable in the evening when demand is usually higher, the report added.
“Curtailment is no longer a hypothetical. It is already visible in high-renewable states, and instances of low or near-zero midday power prices on the exchanges are becoming more frequent,” said Simarpreet Singh of Hartek Power. “These carry real financial consequences for developers, particularly where curtailed generation goes uncompensated.”
Zero prices
India has met only about 80% of its annual transmission targets over the past five years, according to Ember. As a result, the target for the inter-state transmission system, which is crucial for evacuating power from solar-rich states to other states, has increased from 15,382 circuit kilometres to 25,146 ckm for FY27.
Ember added that about 20 GW of renewable energy capacity is likely to face connectivity delays of more than four months in FY27 because of slow installation of transmission capacity.
Inadequate energy storage has also led to an oversupply of solar power, primarily between 11 am and 3.30 pm, forcing discoms into distress sales on power exchanges, according to executives with power developers.
Power prices fell below ₹0.05 per unit 31 times in the first quarter of FY27, hitting zero on 1 May, according to data from the Indian Energy Exchange. In the year-earlier first quarter, power prices had dropped below ₹0.05 per unit six times.
“When solar supply floods the grid, it results in lower price discovery on energy exchanges as observed on the IEX day-ahead market, where mid-day prices fell to between ₹0 and ₹0.30/kWh on several days in late May and early June 2025,” said Anujesh Dwivedi, partner, Deloitte India.

climate-energy-91bc159fa5.headline: India's Largest Utility Signs PPA With Virginia-Based Solar Group, Will Use Advanced CSP Technology
climate-energy-91bc159fa5.fulltext:
NTPC Limited, India’s largest electric utility, has signed a power purchase agreement with 247 Solar and will deploy that company’s Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) technology as part of its energy strategy.
The companies on October 15 said it will mark the first commercial project for 247 Solar and its solar thermal tech. The Virginia-based company has said the deal is a milestone as 247 Solar improves on the first generation of its technology, which is designed to overcome the intermittency of conventional solar power.
NTPC said it will test whether 247 Solar’s system can help the utility reduce its reliance on coal-fired power generation as India expands its use of renewable energy. Officials said the project, if successful, would likely enable an expansion of 247 Solar’s technology across India.
Advanced CSP
“This new version of solar thermal solves the problem of intermittent solar and wind power, and avoids spending more on outdated, costly, and dirty coal plants,” said Bruce Anderson, founder and CEO of 247Solar. “India’s rapid growth plainly requires more clean, reliable and affordable energy. Our system can help meet that demand. I’m thrilled that after several years of deep due diligence, NTPC is working with us to bring this promising technology into wider use.”
247Solar has said its technology removes the drawbacks of previous CSP technology. The system still captures the sun’s heat with mirrors focused on towers, but the new version is simplified, modular, and scalable. It simultaneously provides heat up to 1,000C (more than 1,800F) for industrial processes, according to the company.
The system, according to 247 Solar, “stores heat for up to 20 hours in ceramic pellets, using hot air to generate electricity around the clock with unique turbines that operate without combustion under normal conditions. If the stored heat runs low overnight or during extended cloudy weather, the same turbines can also run on liquid or gaseous fuels, including natural gas, green hydrogen, or diesel, so the plant can keep producing power without interruption.”
247 Solar said the new technology has several benefits compared with traditional CSP:
- Lower cost.
- Speed to power.
- Simplicity of design and operation.
- High reliability.
- Grid independence.
- Cost-effective baseload power.
The company said the NTPC project is a ~1MW hybrid, integrating one 400-kW modular 247Solar Plant with several hundred kilowatts of photovoltaic solar. It is being installed at Rajasthan’s Bhadla Solar Park, which is among the world’s largest solar energy hubs, in an arid region in northwestern India. The project is backed by the Rajasthan Renewable Energy Corporation Limited, which has approved preliminary studies, site surveys, and structural tests. NTPC and 247Solar said the companies selected the location for its abundant sunshine, and for its easy interconnection for offtake of its energy output.
The groups said the demonstration “marks an early step toward round-the-clock clean power for industry and residents in India,” and added that “success will position Rajasthan as a proving ground for the technology and give NTPC a new tool as it works to meet the country’s growing power demand while reducing reliance on coal, cutting costs and carbon emissions simultaneously.”
—Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

global-economics-ab617f9ddb.headline: Indian IT giants' H-1B visa registrations fall amid Trump's crackdown; Infosys, Cognizant, TCS report fewer entries
global-economics-ab617f9ddb.fulltext:
Swati GandhiPublished19 Oct 2026, 10:36 AM IST As US President Donald Trump's administration tightens immigration policies, including a $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B applications and a wage-weighted selection system introduced for fiscal year 2027, H-1B registrations by major IT companies such as Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) have dropped in the FY2027 lottery. According to data in a Congressional Research Service (CRS) report published on 14 October, Cognizant submitted 100% fewer registrations than in the previous year, while Infosys' registrations declined by 91% and TCS's plunged by 95%. The report, "H-1B Executive Actions in 2026", comes at a time when the Trump administration has announced changes to H-1B visa selection and fees as the government seeks to prioritise higher-paid workers and address what it calls abuse of the programme. According to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), the company-level figures highlight the scale of the decline. Infosys submitted 759 registrations for FY2027, down from 8,886 in FY2026, while TCS’s total declined to 284 from 5,955. Cognizant recorded no registrations, compared with 3,752 the previous year. A Federal Register publication dated 23 September 2026 also highlighted the decline, reporting that combined H-1B registrations by the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms fell by roughly 92%, from 24,946 to 2,055. The figures cover entries in the annual H-1B cap selection process, rather than the companies’ total H-1B workforce. They do not indicate that current visa holders have lost their immigration status. According to the CRS report, the wage-weighted selection system, introduced by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in February this year, was used for the FY2027 H-1B lottery. The fiscal year began this month. The weighted selection process is designed to favour highly skilled and higher-paid workers. Employers have also faced a $100,000 fee introduced last September for certain new H-1B workers entering the US from abroad. In the first eight months after it took effect, initial H-1B petitions requesting consular processing from employers exempt from the annual visa cap fell by 91% compared with the same period a year earlier. According to a Hindustan Times report, the sharp decline in registrations may indicate that Indian IT firms are changing how they staff US projects, potentially placing greater reliance on workers already in the country, visa extensions, transfers and local recruitment. Infosys, TCS and Cognizant reduced fresh registrations against a backdrop of rising costs and changes to the H-1B selection process. While the registration figures alone cannot establish the number of jobs lost or how many Indian professionals will ultimately be able to work in the US, they indicate a substantial decline in fresh lottery registrations by some of the largest IT companies employing Indian professionals, despite Indians accounting for the biggest share of H-1B visa holders in the US. agritech-a589449f11.headline: India's reservoirs remain 31% below full capacity after monsoon; southern states face water shortages
agritech-a589449f11.fulltext:
Water
India's reservoirs remain 31% below full capacity after monsoon; southern states face water shortages
Water storage in 178 major reservoirs is 24.53% lower than a year ago, with the Pennar and Cauvery river basins facing particularly severe deficits
Listen to this article
Summary
- India's reservoirs are 31% below full capacity post-monsoon, with southern states facing acute water shortages.
- Major reservoirs like Aliyar, Somasila, and Mettur report critically low levels, raising concerns over irrigation, drinking water, and hydropower.
- Regional disparities highlight severe deficits in Pennar and Cauvery basins, while Narmada and Mahanadi basins show surplus storage.
Monsoon 2026 has ended, but many of India's reservoirs have not filled to capacity. Across the country's 178 major reservoirs, water storage remains about 31 per cent below full capacity, raising concerns over water availability in the coming months.
According to the Central Water Commission's (CWC) Reservoir Storage Bulletin released on Thursday, 15 October 2026, the 178 reservoirs held 126.717 billion cubic metres (BCM) of water, representing 68.58 per cent of their total usable storage capacity. This means that 31.42 per cent of their combined capacity remained unfilled.
The bulletin showed that water storage was 41.193 BCM, or 24.53 per cent, lower than during the same period last year. It was also 24.930 BCM, or 16.44 per cent, below normal levels, calculated using the average storage recorded over the past 10 years.
The CWC monitors water levels in 178 major reservoirs across India and publishes a weekly bulletin every Thursday. Together, these reservoirs have a usable storage capacity of 184.762 BCM, accounting for about 71.67 per cent of the country's total usable reservoir storage capacity of 257.812 BCM.
Water levels in several major reservoirs have fallen to less than half their normal storage levels. Data from the bulletin showed particularly severe shortages in reservoirs across Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Telangana.
The Aliyar reservoir in Tamil Nadu, recorded no water storage relative to its normal level, placing it at the bottom of the list of reservoirs with less than 50 per cent of normal storage.
In Andhra Pradesh, the Somasila reservoir held 22.05 per cent of its normal storage, while Srisailam stood at 33.64 per cent. Tamil Nadu's Mettur reservoir had 32.49 per cent of normal storage, while Kerala's Idukki reservoir had just 10.62 per cent.
Several reservoirs in Maharashtra also recorded substantial deficits. Jaikwadi held 15.55 per cent of normal storage, Ujani 10.62 per cent, Manjra 12.45 per cent and Lower Terna 28.24 per cent.
In Karnataka, Ghataprabha, Tungabhadra and Sholayar recorded 22.56 per cent, 22.54 per cent and 23.62 per cent of normal storage, respectively. Kerala's Periyar reservoir held 46.43 per cent of its normal storage.
The figures indicate that water availability in several reservoirs across southern and western India remains well below normal levels.
The bulletin also identified 42 reservoirs with water storage between 50 per cent and 80 per cent of normal levels. Of these, 11 had between 51 per cent and 60 per cent of normal storage, 14 had between 61 per cent and 70 per cent, and 17 had between 71 per cent and 80 per cent.
Meanwhile, 12 of the 20 reservoirs associated with hydropower projects had storage levels at or below normal, raising concerns over potential effects on irrigation, drinking water supplies and electricity generation.
A river basin-wise assessment showed that water storage in the Pennar and Cauvery basins fell into the highly deficient category.
The Indus, Mahi, Krishna and Sabarmati basins, along with the Kutch-Saurashtra and Luni river regions, were classified as deficient. Water shortages were also recorded in the east-flowing river basins between Pennar and Kanyakumari and the west-flowing basins between Tadri and Kanyakumari.
In contrast, water storage in the Narmada, Mahanadi and Swarnarekha basins was above normal.
Several other river basins, including the Ganga, Tapti, Godavari, Brahmaputra and Brahmani-Baitarani, had storage levels close to normal.
The figures highlight significant regional differences in India's reservoir storage, with particularly large deficits in southern river basins.
The Cauvery basin recorded a 60.50 per cent deficit compared with normal storage, while the Pennar basin had a deficit of 72.32 per cent. The Krishna basin recorded a 32.59 per cent deficit and the Sabarmati basin a 38.03 per cent deficit.
By comparison, water storage in the Narmada basin was 7.81 per cent above normal. The Mahanadi basin recorded a surplus of 2.95 per cent, while the Swarnarekha basin had 30.74 per cent more water than normal.

agritech-aaa9ae1e74.headline: Russia-Ukraine war: Zelenskyy seeks India’s help to reopen Black Sea grain route — why Delhi’s role matters
agritech-aaa9ae1e74.fulltext:
Bhanu PratapPublished19 Oct 2026, 06:23 PM IST Ukraine is holding talks with India, Turkey and Egypt on restoring safe commercial navigation in the Black Sea, as Russian attacks on port infrastructure and merchant vessels disrupt agricultural exports, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Bloomberg News. The proposed arrangement seeks to protect ships carrying food cargoes through Ukrainian and Russian ports. However, Russia has not agreed to the proposal, despite diplomatic efforts involving the three countries, Zelenskyy said. India’s involvement is significant because New Delhi is engaging with both Moscow and Kyiv on the safety of merchant shipping and the movement of essential supplies. The discussions also highlight the intersection of the Russia-Ukraine war and global food security. Under the proposal outlined by Zelenskyy, India, Turkey and Egypt have suggested that ships sailing under their respective flags should be allowed to call at Ukrainian and Russian ports to transport food cargoes. The arrangement would require assurances that participating vessels would not be attacked, as per Bloomberg. However, the proposal remains uncertain as Russia has not agreed to the suggested arrangement, according to Zelenskyy. New Delhi has separately confirmed that it is in discussions with Moscow and Kyiv on a ceasefire proposal covering the safety of merchant shipping in the Black Sea and the unimpeded movement of grain and energy supplies. On 7 October, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said it was engaging with both sides on the issue. Ukraine’s Black Sea ports are its main gateway for agricultural exports and can handle up to 40 million tonnes of grain during a marketing season. But Russian attacks on port infrastructure and vessels have disrupted shipments, leaving Ukraine struggling to move agricultural cargoes at its usual scale. “We cannot manage this volume of shipments by rail,” Zelenskyy said, underlining the limitations of land-based transport as a substitute for maritime trade. other-interests-cdbbbe709a.headline: It’s about to get a lot harder to keep countries honest about climate change
other-interests-cdbbbe709a.fulltext:
A delay in publishing a scientific report doesn’t usually have serious ramifications for the future of life on Earth. But an impasse between governments over when climate scientists should publish their next landmark assessment of climate change threatens to do just that.
A critical meeting of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, was suspended on 16 October without an agreement on when the results of its seventh assessment cycle – called AR7 – should be made public.
Don’t be fooled by its less than catchy title. AR7 will consist of a series of high-profile scientific reports that will summarise the latest evidence on the threat posed by climate change, how countries should adapt and the emissions cuts needed to remain within safe climatic bounds. Its findings will make headlines around the world and create huge public and media pressure on countries to step up their efforts to fight climate change.
Advertisement
The meeting in Addis Ababa was a last-chance opportunity to ensure the findings of AR7 are published in time for a crucial UN-led “global stocktake” in 2028, when countries are due to evaluate global progress towards cutting emissions.
This process takes place every five years and is meant to inform the next round of national climate goals that countries submit under the Paris Agreement. The regular stocktakes are designed to ratchet up pressure on countries to bolster their carbon-cutting ambition at regular intervals, closing the gap between projected global emissions and the goal of keeping global warming in relation to pre-industrial levels “well below” 2°C.
The last global stocktake took place in 2023, just months after the IPCC had finished reporting the results of its last assessment, AR6. The COP28 summit in Dubai – which marked the culmination of the stocktake – resulted in an international commitment for countries to transition away from fossil fuels, plus new global targets to triple renewable energy capacity and double energy efficiency improvement rates by 2030. Would these targets have been set without the public pressure generated by the IPCC findings?
Of course, countries can get information on the state of the climate, and the measures needed to mitigate and adapt to a warming world, from places other than the IPCC. The deluge of journal articles, summary reports and UN papers provides no shortage of data and analysis for those who want to find it, for the global stocktake or any other purpose. But an IPCC report has gravitas other missives can’t match, and generates the media interest that puts climate change at the forefront of public consciousness ahead of COP summits.
Without a headline-grabbing IPCC report, countries will be under far less pressure to make fresh climate commitments. “It impedes global ambition,” says Richard Allan at the University of Reading, UK, and a lead author for AR7.
So why the delay? A small group of countries, including Russia and Saudi Arabia, are arguing that low-income countries need more time to properly review the IPCC findings before publication.
Their tactics mirror those used in climate summit negotiating rooms, where fossil fuel-dependent countries have, for years, sought to delay and obstruct proceedings to slow international action on cutting emissions. “It’s obviously a delaying tactic,” says Bob Watson, a former chair of the IPCC. “Those countries that want action fundamentally want these reports before this global stocktake. Those countries that don’t want action… they don’t want to see those reports because they know what they’ll say is we’re not on target for 1.5°C or even 2°C”.
It is now looking increasingly unlikely that the IPCC will be able to agree on a publication timetable that will align with the global stocktake. In a statement published on Monday, IPCC chair Jim Skea said he will reconvene the meeting “at the earliest opportunity” to push for a decision. A likely outcome now is that a report on the science of climate change – the least contentious of the three parts – may arrive in May 2028, with two further reports, which assess adaptation and mitigation, published the following year.
“It is an unhelpful fracturing of the process,” says Gareth Redmond-King at UK think tank the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit. Without the IPCC underscoring the urgency of the crisis, there is a risk that “countries can behave as though the pressure is eased”, he warns.

Blueprint is a one-week digital hackathon for secondary school students, organized by FUSE Society in partnership with Free Geek.
Participants will identify a business challenge facing a real company and design a digital solution to address it, demonstrating analytical rigour, creativity, and commercial judgment. Each team will submit a solution together with a recorded presentation explaining the work. The winning team will receive a grand prize of $250.
No prior programming experience is required. Under the core evaluation criteria, submissions are assessed on the quality of the analysis and the suitability of the proposed solution rather than on technical polish, and a clickable prototype produced in a design tool is scored on equal terms with a coded application.
A separate Technical Execution bonus of up to [10] points is available at both judging stages to teams submitting a functioning technical build. The bonus is additional to the core criteria, is capped at [10] points of a possible [100], and is never used to resolve a tie between teams.
A complete submission consists of three components. All three must be finished by the Day 7 deadline. A Devpost project page alone does not constitute a submission.
Each team must publish a project page to the Blueprint hackathon page. The page must state the problem identified, the proposed solution, an implementation outline addressing cost and timeline, and the names of all team members. The solution artifact must be attached to or linked from this page, whether as an uploaded file, an embedded design link, or a repository link. The project page must be published rather than saved as a draft.
Each team must record a presentation of no more than 8 minutes explaining the solution and the reasoning behind it. Where practical, each team member should appear or speak.
The recording must be uploaded to YouTube with the visibility set to Unlisted. Recordings set to Private cannot be accessed by the judging panel and will not be scored. Teams are advised to test the link in a private browsing window before submitting.
The submission form is the step that formally enters a team into the competition. The form requires the team name; the names, ages, schools, and countries of all members; a team contact email address; the Devpost project link; the YouTube presentation link; an artificial intelligence usage disclosure; and confirmation that the team has read and accepts these rules.
A confirmation email will be sent within 24 hours of submission. Teams that do not receive confirmation should contact the Organizers immediately rather than assume the submission was received.
Teams may resubmit the form at any point before the deadline; the most recent entry will be treated as final.

ai-85e6cdf454.headline: Ex-OpenAI employee accused of planting device has Saudi backing: Prosecutor
ai-85e6cdf454.fulltext:
Ex-OpenAI employee accused of planting device has Saudi backing: Prosecutor
US federal prosecutors allege the defendant was in frequent contact with unnamed member of royal family.
An ex-OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company appears to have received considerable support from the Saudi government, United States prosecutors have said in a court filing.
Federal prosecutors allege that the defendant, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was in frequent communication with an unnamed member of the Saudi royal family and that a Saudi military official paid for a one-way plane ticket for Alfozan’s wife and young son to return to Saudi Arabia after his arrest, according to the court document, made public late on Sunday.
Prosecutors made those allegations as they asked a federal judge to keep Alfozan in US custody to await trial, arguing he is a flight risk. Alfozan, a Saudi national and lawful permanent resident in the US, is scheduled to appear in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday.
The case has highlighted security challenges around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for an edge in the transformational technology.
“The defendant went to significant lengths to create customized, encrypted recording devices to secretly record highly sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives, high-level business counterparts, and government officials, all while communicating with individuals of significance in Saudi Arabia and pursuing opportunities in — and making plans to travel to — Saudi Arabia,” prosecutors wrote in a detention memo.
The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A lawyer for Alfozan did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The lawyer, William Pernik, previously asked for Alfozan to be released from custody, subject to conditions including location monitoring and surrendering his passport, and said Alfozan had spent the last 15 years in the US and had applied to become a citizen.
The lawyer said a planned trip by Alfozan to Saudi Arabia this month was booked before he was under investigation and was for “family and immigration reasons”, according to a court filing.
Investigation remains active
US prosecutors charged Alfozan last week with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan plugged a recording device into the back of a television in an executive conference room at one of OpenAI’s San Francisco buildings, according to a criminal complaint.
Meetings involving government officials took place in the conference room around the time the device was installed, according to the prosecutors’ detention memo.
Prosecutors said the investigation remains active and additional charges could be brought against Alfozan.
A member of the Saudi royal family sought to recruit Alfozan for an AI-focused role in Saudi Arabia, writing in one message, “Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!” Alfozan replied, “100,” according to messages cited by prosecutors.
Before his arrest, Alfozan was scheduled to fly to Riyadh during a planned two-month parental leave. His wife told investigators that she and their son planned to move permanently to Saudi Arabia and that Alfozan eventually intended to join them, according to prosecutors.
In an Arabic-language interview on the Identity Capital podcast last month, Alfozan said that he visits Saudi Arabia three or four times a year, follows developments there and advises or mentors Saudi startups.
He said meeting Prince Mohammed bin Salman, then deputy crown prince, during a 2016 gathering with young Saudi tech workers in Silicon Valley persuaded him to learn at a top tech company before bringing those skills back home.
While Alfozan was working at Facebook, he and other Saudis in Silicon Valley formed a consulting initiative that linked Saudi public- and private-sector organisations with expertise in big data, the internet of things and machine learning.
OpenAI previously said it discovered the device on September 30 and referred the matter to the FBI.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the Saudi embassy for comment.

ai-b0fb4c0567.fulltext:
A little over a month ago, Anthropic and AI infrastructure provider Nscale announced a $45 billion compute deal. Now, the duo may be about to do it again.
Bloomberg reports that the two companies are said to be on the verge of announcing yet another $45 billion compute deal, citing people familiar with the matter. Those sources cautioned that talks are still under way and that the details could change.
If the deal goes through, it would be the latest in a long string of giant compute deals Anthropic has struck over the past year. TechCrunch reached out to Nscale and Anthropic for more information and will update this story if we hear back.
The massive amount of money being sunk into AI compute deals has spooked a certain segment of investors, who worry that companies are spending too much money for too little profit. Still, Anthropic has pressed on with such partnerships, driven by the belief that it will all pay off in the end.
Both Anthropic and Nscale are also currently pursuing IPOs. Anthropic is still expected to go public this year. Nscale is also seeking to go public, although Bloomberg reported today that the company is experiencing investor pushback over its proposed valuation of $30 billion.

ai-ba4c6fde36.headline: Nscale, Anthropic in Talks for $45 Billion Cloud Computing Deal
ai-ba4c6fde36.fulltext:
Signage on a fence at a Nscale data center project in Barstow, Texas.
Nscale Ltd., the AI cloud computing firm, is in talks to sell computing power to Anthropic PBC in a deal that could be worth about $45 billion, according to people familiar with the negotiations.
The Nvidia Corp.-backed data center developer is seeking a second major deal with the firm behind Claude for a second facility at its Monarch data center campus in West Virginia, the people said. Anthropic has agreements in place with Nscale for infrastructure that’s worth as much as about $44.6 billion, according to a regulatory filing for Nscale’s planned initial public offering.

ai-6c15f816f3.headline: Z.AI Founders Worked on Research Funded by China Institute That UK Tied to Spies
ai-6c15f816f3.fulltext:
Four founders of one of China’s most promising artificial intelligence companies, Z.AI Co., worked on research in a joint project with a technology institute that the UK government accused of having “very strong ties” to China’s main spy agency, according to publicly available research papers from China and an “espionage alert” from the UK.
The nearly four-year-long AI research project, which overlapped with the company’s start in 2019, was co-funded by Beijing-based China General Technology Research Institute, or CGTRI, and the National Natural Science Foundation of China, according to a previously unreported 78-page report that the project’s leaders compiled to detail their findings. A CGTRI engineer and one of Z.AI’s founders were among the project’s leaders, and three other Z.AI founders contributed to the research, according to the report.

work-careers-1402dca8fd.headline: Infosys, TCS and Cognizant cut H-1B lottery registrations as Trump tightens US visa rules
work-careers-1402dca8fd.fulltext:
Three major IT services companies with extensive operations in India have sharply reduced their participation in the US H-1B visa lottery, with Cognizant submitting no registrations for the fiscal year 2027 lottery, according to a report by the Congressional Research Service (CRS).
Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), which were among the companies with the highest numbers of entries in the previous year's lottery, recorded declines of 100 per cent, 91 per cent and 95 per cent, respectively, the report said. The CRS published its report, H-1B Executive Actions in 2026, on October 14.
Also read: Mutual fund holdings of IT stocks sink to record low in September
The figures come as US President Donald Trump's administration introduces changes to the H-1B programme, which allows American employers to hire foreign professionals for jobs requiring specialised knowledge and a university degree. The measures include higher potential hiring costs, changes to how applicants are selected and closer scrutiny of employers.
The report identifies the sharp fall in registrations as evidence that companies which previously entered large numbers of candidates into the lottery are now submitting significantly fewer entries. However, it does not establish that the immigration crackdown alone caused the decline or explain the individual decisions made by the three companies.
Why US companies face higher H-1B hiring costs
One of the most significant changes came in September 2025, when the Trump administration introduced a $100,000 fee for US employers petitioning to bring certain new H-1B workers from abroad. The fee was in effect for most of the following year but is temporarily blocked amid ongoing litigation, the CRS report said.
In August 2026, the Department of Homeland Security proposed a separate fee of $103,265 for each H-1B petition subject to the annual visa cap. This is a proposal and is distinct from the earlier $100,000 fee.
The Department of Labour has also proposed increasing the minimum wages employers must offer H-1B workers. The proposed changes would raise the wage benchmarks at all four skill levels, from entry-level positions to the most experienced roles. The department estimates that the changes could increase employers' costs by about $1.46 billion in the first year.
For IT services companies that hire professionals for projects in the US, such measures could make overseas recruitment more expensive and affect decisions about how and where to deploy employees. However, the report does not quantify the financial impact on Infosys, TCS or Cognizant individually.
Also read: US suspends TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant and three other firms from PERM green card programme
H-1B lottery now favours higher-paid workers
The US has also changed how candidates are selected for H-1B visas. In February 2026, the Department of Homeland Security introduced a weighted selection system to favour higher-skilled and higher-paid workers, replacing the previous random selection process. The new system first applied to the lottery for employment starting in October 2026.
This change is important because selection is no longer based solely on a random draw. The new approach gives greater weight to higher-paid positions, potentially affecting employers' recruitment strategies and the types of roles for which they seek visas.
The administration has also increased scrutiny of companies hiring foreign workers. In July 2026, the Department of Labour announced an investigation into suspected fraud, human trafficking and coercive wage kickbacks in the H-1B programme. Its enforcement efforts build on Project Firewall, launched in 2025 to investigate suspected violations, including the displacement of US workers and inadequate recruitment of American candidates.
In September 2026, Trump issued an executive order directing agencies to consider whether employers sponsoring H-1B workers had carried out or planned layoffs during the preceding year when assessing relevant applications and petitions.
What the decline means for Indian IT professionals
The steep fall in registrations by the three companies highlights the changing environment for Indian technology professionals seeking to work in the US through employer-sponsored visas. The impact, however, cannot be measured by lottery registrations alone.
An H-1B registration is an entry into the selection process, not an approved visa or a confirmed job placement. Fewer registrations therefore do not automatically mean that the same proportion of visas or jobs has been lost.
The CRS report also found that initial H-1B petitions requiring consular processing from employers exempt from the annual visa cap fell by 91 per cent during the first eight months in which the $100,000 fee was in effect, compared with the same period a year earlier.
Taken together, these figures point to a significant change in employer participation amid tighter US immigration rules. For Indian professionals, the developments underline the importance of understanding how employer sponsorship, salary levels and visa eligibility may affect opportunities to work in the US.

work-careers-a1bcc6a209.headline: Indian IT giants' H-1B visa registrations fall amid Trump's crackdown; Infosys, Cognizant, TCS report fewer entries
work-careers-a1bcc6a209.fulltext:
Swati GandhiPublished19 Oct 2026, 10:36 AM IST As US President Donald Trump's administration tightens immigration policies, including a $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B applications and a wage-weighted selection system introduced for fiscal year 2027, H-1B registrations by major IT companies such as Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) have dropped in the FY2027 lottery. According to data in a Congressional Research Service (CRS) report published on 14 October, Cognizant submitted 100% fewer registrations than in the previous year, while Infosys' registrations declined by 91% and TCS's plunged by 95%. The report, "H-1B Executive Actions in 2026", comes at a time when the Trump administration has announced changes to H-1B visa selection and fees as the government seeks to prioritise higher-paid workers and address what it calls abuse of the programme. According to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), the company-level figures highlight the scale of the decline. Infosys submitted 759 registrations for FY2027, down from 8,886 in FY2026, while TCS’s total declined to 284 from 5,955. Cognizant recorded no registrations, compared with 3,752 the previous year. A Federal Register publication dated 23 September 2026 also highlighted the decline, reporting that combined H-1B registrations by the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms fell by roughly 92%, from 24,946 to 2,055. The figures cover entries in the annual H-1B cap selection process, rather than the companies’ total H-1B workforce. They do not indicate that current visa holders have lost their immigration status. According to the CRS report, the wage-weighted selection system, introduced by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in February this year, was used for the FY2027 H-1B lottery. The fiscal year began this month. The weighted selection process is designed to favour highly skilled and higher-paid workers. Employers have also faced a $100,000 fee introduced last September for certain new H-1B workers entering the US from abroad. In the first eight months after it took effect, initial H-1B petitions requesting consular processing from employers exempt from the annual visa cap fell by 91% compared with the same period a year earlier. According to a Hindustan Times report, the sharp decline in registrations may indicate that Indian IT firms are changing how they staff US projects, potentially placing greater reliance on workers already in the country, visa extensions, transfers and local recruitment. Infosys, TCS and Cognizant reduced fresh registrations against a backdrop of rising costs and changes to the H-1B selection process. While the registration figures alone cannot establish the number of jobs lost or how many Indian professionals will ultimately be able to work in the US, they indicate a substantial decline in fresh lottery registrations by some of the largest IT companies employing Indian professionals, despite Indians accounting for the biggest share of H-1B visa holders in the US. work-careers-a548a69dc5.headline: Infosys, Cognizant and TCS H-1B visa registrations plunge amid Trump’s US immigration crackdown | Hindustan Times
work-careers-a548a69dc5.fulltext:
Infosys, Cognizant and TCS H-1B visa registrations plunge amid Trump’s US immigration crackdown
Infosys, TCS and Cognizant together submitted far fewer H-1B registrations for the FY2027 lottery, with Cognizant registering none.
H-1B visa registrations by major Indian IT companies Infosys, Cognizant and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) plunged in the US financial year 2027 lottery, reflecting the impact of tighter immigration rules and rising costs for employers under President Donald Trump’s administration.
According to a Congressional Research Service (CRS) report, Cognizant submitted 100% fewer registrations than in the previous year, while Infosys registrations fell 91% and those from TCS declined 95%.
The report comes as the US administration has introduced changes to H-1B visa selection and fees, seeking to prioritize higher-paid workers and address what it describes as abuse of the program.
H-1B registrations fall sharply at Indian IT companies
The company-level figures show the scale of the decline. Infosys registrations dropped from 8,886 in FY2026 to 759 in FY2027, while TCS registrations fell from 5,955 to 284. Cognizant went from 3,752 registrations to zero, according to figures from the USCIS technical appendix, detailed in this analysis of the data.
Also read: US legal immigration falls by half under Trump as visa restrictions hit 91 countries
The wider trend is also visible in an official Federal Register publication dated September 23, 2026. It said the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms together reduced H-1B registrations from 24,946 to 2,055, a decline of about 92%.
These figures refer to registrations submitted for the annual H-1B cap lottery. They do not represent the total number of H-1B workers employed by these companies, nor do they mean existing visa holders have lost their status.
Higher fees and a weighted lottery reshape hiring
The FY2027 lottery was the first to use a weighted selection process designed to favor higher-skilled and higher-paid workers. The change was introduced in February 2026, according to the CRS report.
Employers have also faced the impact of a $100,000 payment introduced in September 2025 for certain new H-1B workers coming from abroad. The CRS report said that during the first eight months the payment was in effect, initial H-1B petitions for consular processing from cap-exempt employers fell 91% compared with the same period a year earlier.
The administration has also proposed further changes. In August 2026, the Department of Homeland Security proposed a separate $103,265 fee for H-1B petitions. The proposal is outlined in the Federal Register notice. This is a proposed fee, not a final rule.
Also read: New US bill targets H-1B salary threshold, proposing an increase to nearly $140,000
Meanwhile, the Department of Labor proposed raising prevailing-wage requirements in March 2026. The CRS report estimated that the changes could increase employer costs by approximately $1.46 billion in the first year.
What the decline means for Indian IT workers
The steep fall in registrations could signal a shift in how Indian IT companies staff US projects, with employers potentially relying more on workers already in the country, visa extensions, transfers and local hiring. Companies such as Infosys, TCS and Cognizant had cut fresh registrations amid higher costs and changes to the lottery system.
However, registration figures alone do not establish how many jobs have been lost or how many Indian professionals will ultimately work in the US. They point to a substantial reduction in fresh lottery entries by some of the largest Indian IT employers as the costs and rules surrounding overseas recruitment change.

world-653356d171.fulltext:
[Text below is The Japan Times's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
SINGAPORE/JAKARTA – Muhamad Yasin, a 63-year-old parking attendant in central Jakarta, says he has cut back on meals as rising prices have put food staples beyond his reach.
“I used to be able to get rice, tempeh and tofu for 7,000 to 8,000 rupiah ($0.39 to $0.44). Now, it’s 15,000 rupiah,” said Yasin, who earns 200,000 to 300,000 rupiah a week, beside the minimarket where he watches over parked motorcycles.
Global food inflation is poised to accelerate in the coming months and persist well into 2027, as war-related shipping disruptions and El Nino-driven drought squeeze cereal supplies, putting additional pressure on vulnerable consumers like Yasin, a father of four.
